feedback: If the child writes 3+4 (rows plus row-size): shade one row to show it holds 4, then show that same 4 repeats for every row → 4+4+4. Name clearly that 'number of rows' and 'amount in each row' are two different things; the equation adds the row-amount once per row.

If the child gives the correct sum but justifies it only as 'because it makes 12': cover the rows one at a time so each shows the same 4, and name that the rows being equal is exactly what lets you add 4 repeatedly instead of counting every dot.

If the child insists on counting every dot and distrusts the shortcut: do NOT force the shortcut. Let them verify by counting a few arrays so repeated addition earns their trust over several examples.

For the ragged arrangement: confirm that because the rows are not equal you cannot write one repeated-equal-addend equation, so it is not a multiplication situation — this is the point of the contrast.
activities.intendedInsight: Each equal row of an array is one equal addend, so adding the rows gives the total; the multiplication fact is just the shorthand for adding equal rows, and this only works when the rows are equal.
learnerActions: Look at a 3×4 array (3 rows, 4 dots in each row) and point to one row to establish that it holds 4 dots.
Add the array one row at a time, saying and writing the running total: 4, then 4+4, then 4+4+4 = 12 — one addend per row.
After writing 4+4+4=12, write the matching multiplication 3×4=12 and say which number tells how many rows and which tells how many are in each row.
Read the same array by columns instead and write it as 3+3+3+3 (four 3s), noticing you get 12 again.
Now try a ragged arrangement where one row has 4 and another has 5; attempt to write a single equal-addend equation and explain why it will not form.
activities.title: Sum the rows: build the equal-addend equation from an array

feedback: If the number of rows and the amount per row get swapped, have the child count the addends in the equation (how many 5s? four) and match that to the number of rows drawn.
If rows are drawn unequal, point out that the equation uses the same number each time, so every row must hold the same amount.
activities.intendedInsight: Children can move in both directions — from array to equation and from equation to array — which shows they understand the equal-groups structure rather than just reading one off the other.
learnerActions: Given the equation 5+5+5+5, draw a rectangular array that matches it (four rows of five, or equivalently five columns of four).
Say aloud which part of the equation is the number of rows and which is the amount in each row.
Write the multiplication fact for your array (4×5 or 5×4) and check the total matches 20.
Explain why your drawing shows equal rows and how that connects back to the repeated addition.
activities.title: Draw an array for a given equation

feedback: If a learner picks the unequal-addend distractor, draw the arrangement that equation would represent and shade its rows to show they are not equal, so it does not match the equal-rows array and cannot be written as one repeated-equal-addend equation.
If the addition and multiplication are seen as unrelated, place 4+4+4 beside 3×4 and count: three rows, four in each — the multiplication summarises the addition.
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising and completing the correct equal-addend equation (and rejecting an unequal-addend distractor) confirms the array-to-repeated-addition bridge and the equal-addends requirement.
learnerActions: For a shown array, fill in the blanks of the equal-addend equation (__ + __ + __ = __).
Write the matching multiplication fact for the same array.

From a set of candidate equations, choose the one that matches a given equal-rows array; include a distractor that uses unequal addends (e.g., 3+4+5), which would correspond to a ragged arrangement and does not match.
Explain why the unequal-addend distractor cannot represent the equal-rows array as a single equal-addend equation.
activities.title: Match and complete: array ↔ equal-addend equation ↔ multiplication
